items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we want to solve the quadratic equation
[MATH: x^2 -2x +2=0.]

Content:
This quadratic is written in standard form with [MATH: a=1,] [MATH: b=-2,] and [MATH: c=2.] However, its discriminant is negative:
[MATH: b^{2} − 4ac|= (− 2)^{2} − 4(1)(2); = 4 − 8; = − 4; < 0]

Content:
This means that the quadratic equation has no real solutions. However, if we allow complex solutions, we may solve the equation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x|= (− b ± sqrt(b^{2} − 4ac))/(2a); = (− (− 2) ± sqrt((− 2)^{2} − 4(1)(2)))/(2 ⋅ 1); = (2 ± sqrt(− 4))/(2); = (2 ± 2\textrm{i})/(2); = 1 ± \textrm{i}]

Content:
Therefore, the equation [MATH: x^2 -2x +2=0] has two solutions, [MATH: x=1+\textrm{i}] and [MATH: x=1-\textrm{i}.]

items.title: Solving a Quadratic Equation With Complex Roots Using the Quadratic Formula

sections.normalized_html:
We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula: [MATH: x = \frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}]

In this case, the coefficients are [MATH: a=1, b=-4,] and [MATH: c=5.] Substituting these values into the quadratic formula, we get [MATH: x|= (− (− 4) ± sqrt((− 4)^{2} − 4(1)(5)))/(2(1)); = (4 ± sqrt(16 − 20))/(2); = (4 ± sqrt(− 4))/(2); = (4 ± 2\textrm{i})/(2); = 2 ± \textrm{i}.]

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, [MATH: x=2+\textrm{i}] and [MATH: x=2-\textrm{i}.]

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, [MATH: x=\dfrac{1}{2}+ \sqrt{3} \, \textrm{i}] and [MATH: x=\dfrac{1}{2}- \sqrt{3} \, \textrm{i}.]

sections.readable_text: The equation [MATH: x^2+8x+80=0] can be written in the form [MATH: (x+p)^2=q.] Find [MATH: p+q,] and solve the equation.

sections.normalized_html:
We first move the constant to the right-hand side:

[MATH: x^{2} + 8x + 80|= 0; x^{2} + 8x|= − 80]

Next, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

[MATH: x^{2} + 8x|= − 80; x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 4x + 4^{2} − 4^{2}|= − 80; (x + 4)^{2} − 16|= − 80; (x + 4)^{2}|= − 64]

Therefore, [MATH: p=4,] [MATH: q=-64,] and [MATH: p+q = -60.]

Finally, we solve the equation using the square root method:

[MATH: (x + 4)^{2}|= − 64; x + 4|= ± sqrt(− 64); x + 4|= ± 8\textrm{i}; x|= − 4 ± 8\textrm{i}]

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, [MATH: x=-4+8\,\textrm{i}] and [MATH: x=-4-8\,\textrm{i}.]
